learn.title: Iron‑Air Batteries for 100+ Hour Storage
learn.intro: Long‑duration storage is essential for a reliable renewable grid, letting solar and wind power be used when the sun isn’t shining or wind isn’t blowing. Iron‑air batteries store energy for over 100 hours at low cost, using abundant iron and air, making them a promising solution for balancing seasonal variations and supporting grid stability. They can be manufactured using existing steel mills, reducing material costs and enabling rapid deployment across diverse climates.
learn.c1_text: Imagine a giant iron filing that releases energy when air flows through it, like a wind‑up toy that powers a house for days. Each kilogram of iron can store roughly 0.5 kWh, so a 10‑ton system delivers about 5 MWh over 100 hours, enough to power a small village continuously. Providing reliable, low‑cost power for months during low‑renewable periods, avoiding fossil‑fuel backup plants.
learn.c2_text: When air is forced through the iron particles, oxidation reactions release electrons, converting chemical energy directly into electricity without moving parts. This direct conversion yields efficiencies above 30% in labs, comparable to pumped hydro and enabling lightweight, flexible panels for urban rooftops. The cells also maintain high efficiency even at 50°C, making them suitable for hot climates.
learn.c3_title: India's Rooftop Solar and Net Metering 🌞
learn.c3_text: India's rapid rooftop solar adoption, driven by the 2019 Net Metering Policy, lets households export surplus electricity to the grid and earn credits. By 2024, over 3.5 GW of rooftop capacity was installed, enough to power 10 million homes and cut peak demand by 15 GW. This growth supports India's 450 GW renewable target by 2030, boosting energy security and local jobs.
learn.stat1: A 10‑ton iron‑air system can deliver 5 MWh over 100 hours, enough for a small village continuously.
learn.stat2: Round‑trip efficiency ranges from 70% to 80%, comparable to pumped hydro storage.
learn.stat3: Projected costs are $80‑$120 per kWh, significantly lower than lithium‑ion for long‑duration applications.
learn.stat4: Global iron reserves exceed 2 billion tonnes, ensuring scalability for grid‑scale storage.

learn.title: Perovskite Solar Cells — Higher Efficiency 🌞
learn.intro: Perovskite solar cells promise a leap forward in photovoltaic technology, offering higher efficiencies and lower production costs than traditional silicon panels. Their thin‑film nature enables flexible, lightweight modules that can be integrated into building facades, windows, and even fabrics, expanding solar’s reach beyond rooftops.
learn.c1_text: Perovskite cells have reached over 30% efficiency in laboratory settings, compared to about 22% for typical silicon panels. This leap means fewer panels are needed to generate the same amount of electricity, reducing land use and balance‑of‑system costs.
learn.c2_text: Recent advances in encapsulation have extended perovskite lifetimes to over 2,000 hours under continuous illumination, addressing earlier stability concerns. The materials can be printed using roll‑to‑roll techniques, lowering production costs and enabling large‑scale manufacturing.
learn.c3_title: India's Solar Growth and Policy Context 🏙️
learn.c3_text: India added more than 10 GW of new solar capacity in 2023, with rooftop solar growing 70% year‑over‑year under the 2019 net‑metering policy. This rapid expansion helps the country meet its goal of 280 GW solar capacity by 2030.
learn.stat1: Lab‑record perovskite cells have reached 33% efficiency, surpassing typical silicon panels.
learn.stat2: Commercial silicon modules average 22% efficiency, about 11 percentage points lower than the best perovskite cells.
learn.stat4: Manufacturing costs are projected to be 30% lower than silicon modules at scale.

learn.title: Rooftop Solar and Net Metering in India 🌞
learn.intro: Rooftop solar is transforming India’s energy landscape by enabling households to generate clean electricity on-site and export excess power through net metering. This policy framework has accelerated adoption, reducing reliance on centralized generation and empowering consumers to become prosumers.
learn.c1_title: Rooftop Solar and Net Metering in India 🌞
learn.c1_text: India's rapid rooftop solar adoption, driven by the 2019 Net Metering Policy, lets households export surplus electricity to the grid and earn credits. By 2024, over 3.5 GW of rooftop capacity was installed, enough to power 10 million homes and cut peak demand by 15 GW. This expansion supports India's 450 GW renewable target by 2030, boosting energy security and local jobs.
learn.c2_text: The net‑metering policy allows consumers to receive retail‑rate credits for exported electricity, incentivizing self‑generation. Households can offset up to 100% of their electricity bill, leading to average savings of 20‑30% on monthly bills.
learn.c3_text: The rapid growth of rooftop solar reduces reliance on fossil‑fuel peaker plants, cuts CO₂ emissions by an estimated 12 million tonnes annually, and creates local jobs in installation and maintenance.
learn.stat1: Rooftop solar installations in India reached 3.5 GW by 2024, covering over 10 million homes.
learn.stat2: The 2019 net‑metering policy has driven a 45% year‑over‑year increase in rooftop solar installations.
learn.stat3: Rooftop solar now accounts for 12% of India’s total solar capacity, up from 5% in 2019.
learn.stat4: India aims for 450 GW renewable capacity by 2030, with rooftop solar playing a key role.

learn.title: String vs Micro vs Hybrid Inverters Explained 🔌
learn.intro: Inverters are the heart of any solar system, converting DC electricity from panels into usable AC power. Choosing the right inverter type — string, micro, or hybrid — affects system efficiency, shading tolerance, monitoring capabilities, and overall cost.
learn.c1_text: String inverters connect multiple panels in series to a single unit, making installation simple and inexpensive. They are ideal for unshaded roofs with uniform panel orientation and typically cost 15‑30% less than micro inverters.
learn.c2_text: Micro inverters are mounted on each panel, allowing independent operation and maximizing energy harvest even when some panels are shaded. They provide module‑level monitoring and can boost overall system efficiency by up to 25%.
learn.c3_text: Hybrid inverters integrate string and micro technologies, offering the cost benefits of string inverters with the shading tolerance of micro inverters. They support battery backup, making them ideal for homes seeking energy independence.
learn.stat1: String inverters typically cost $0.15 per watt, while micro inverters cost about $0.30 per watt.
learn.stat2: Micro inverters can improve system efficiency by up to 25% compared to string inverters in partially shaded conditions.
learn.stat3: Hybrid inverters reduce installation time by up to 20% compared to using separate string and micro inverters.
learn.stat4: A 5 kW residential string inverter costs roughly $750, while an equivalent micro‑inverter setup costs about $1,500.

learn.title: Second Life EV Batteries for Grid Storage 🚗🔋
learn.intro: Electric vehicle (EV) batteries retain significant capacity after their automotive life, making them perfect candidates for second‑life reuse in grid storage. Reusing these batteries reduces waste, lowers storage costs, and supports the integration of renewable energy into the grid.
learn.c1_title: Second Life EV Batteries – Extending Battery Life ♻️
learn.c1_text: More than 1.2 million EV batteries reached end‑of‑life in 2023, many still holding 70‑80% of their original capacity. These batteries can be repurposed for stationary storage, providing 5‑10 kWh per module for residential or community grid applications.
learn.c2_title: Economic Benefits of Second Life Storage 💰
learn.c2_text: Second‑life batteries can reduce grid storage costs by up to 40% compared with new battery installations, as they leverage existing battery packs with minimal additional hardware. This makes renewable integration more affordable for utilities and microgrid operators.
learn.c3_title: Policy and Market Outlook in India 📈
learn.c3_text: India's rapid EV adoption, with over 1 million EVs on the road by 2024, creates a growing pool of used batteries for grid storage. The government's push for renewable energy and energy storage supports the deployment of second‑life battery projects, aligning with its 2030 renewable targets.
learn.stat1: Over 1.2 million EV batteries were retired in 2023, many retaining 70‑80% capacity.
learn.stat2: A single second‑life battery module can store 5‑10 kWh, enough to power a small home for a day.
learn.stat3: Second‑life batteries can cut grid storage costs by up to 40% compared to new battery systems.
learn.stat4: Global second‑life battery capacity is projected to reach 15 GW by 2030, a tenfold increase from 2020.

learn.title: Microgrids: Energy Independence for Villages 🌍
learn.intro: Microgrids are localized energy grids that can operate independently or in conjunction with the main utility, providing reliable power to villages, disaster‑affected areas, and remote communities. By integrating solar, wind, and storage, microgrids enhance energy independence and resilience.
learn.c1_text: A microgrid typically combines renewable generation (solar PV or wind), energy storage (batteries), and a control system that manages supply and demand. It can island itself during outages, ensuring continuous power to critical loads such as hospitals, schools, and water pumps.
learn.c2_text: Microgrids reduce diesel generator use by up to 60% in off‑grid villages, cutting fuel costs and emissions. They also enable 24‑hour electricity access, which improves education, health outcomes, and local economic activity.
learn.c3_text: The Indian government has launched several microgrid projects in rural states like Bihar and Odisha, aiming to electrify 10 million people by 2025. These projects combine solar PV with battery storage and have already connected over 7 million people to reliable power.
learn.stat1: Microgrids currently serve over 7 million people across India, providing reliable electricity to remote villages.
learn.stat2: The government plans to install 500 MW of microgrid capacity by 2025, up from 150 MW in 2020.
learn.stat3: Microgrids can reduce diesel generator use by 60% in disaster‑prone regions, cutting emissions and fuel expenses.
learn.stat4: A 1 MW microgrid can power approximately 500 homes, supporting community resilience during outages.
